title: Why the Perseids are the Most Famous Meteor Shower
gist: A short explainer on the Perseid meteor shower's annual regularity (peaking August 10-12) and its mythological history, from the Romans' fertility-god Priapus association to its Catholic rebranding as St. Lawrence's Tears.

themes.theme: The Perseids' annual regularity and visibility

insights.claim: The Perseid meteor shower peaks every year around August 10-12 and is a must-see event for Northern Hemisphere stargazers, sometimes producing 50 to 100 fireballs and streaks of light per hour.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Gives skywatchers a reliable annual astronomical event with a predictable, high-visibility peak window each August.
insights.quote: sometimes as many as 50 to 100 per hour
insights.locator: The Perseid meteor showers are beginning to peak

insights.claim: The Perseids take their modern name from the constellation Perseus, the point from which they appear to radiate.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Explains the naming convention used for meteor showers generally, tied to apparent radiant point in the sky.
insights.quote: The Perseids get their modern name from the constellation Perseus, where they appear to originate.
insights.locator: The Perseids get their modern name

insights.claim: The Romans associated the Perseid meteor shower with the minor fertility god Priapus, viewing the meteors as Priapus blessing the fields with his cosmic seed.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Illustrates how pre-modern cultures wove astronomical events into fertility and agricultural belief systems.
insights.quote: To the Romans, the Perseids represented Priapus blessing the fields with his cosmic seed.
insights.locator: The Perseids get their modern name

insights.claim: With the spread of Catholicism, the Perseid meteor shower was rebranded as “St. Lawrence's Tears,” tied to the August 10 feast day honoring St. Lawrence, who was reportedly roasted alive by Roman emperor Valerian.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Shows how religious traditions later overwrote pagan astronomical folklore, giving the same natural event a new cultural meaning tied to the church calendar.
insights.quote: the event became rebranded as “St. Lawrence’s Tears,” in honor of the August 10 feast of St. Lawrence, who was roasted alive by the Roman emperor Valerian
